lessons.title: Aggregate Functions
lessons.concept: Aggregate functions perform calculations on a set of rows and return a single value. Common aggregates are COUNT (number of rows/values), SUM (total), AVG (average), MIN (minimum), and MAX (maximum). Aggregates ignore NULLs in most cases (except COUNT(*) which counts rows).
lessons.formula: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(col) counts non-NULL values; SUM(col), AVG(col), MIN(col), MAX(col) operate on column values.
lessons.worked_example: For values 10, NULL, 20 in a column, COUNT(*) over 3 rows returns 3, COUNT(col) returns 2, SUM(col) returns 30, AVG(col) returns 15.
mistakes: Assuming NULLs are treated as 0 in SUM/AVG
Expecting aggregates to return one value per row without GROUP BY

lessons.title: GROUP BY Clause
lessons.concept: GROUP BY groups rows that share the same values in specified columns so aggregate functions can be applied per group. When GROUP BY is used, selected non-aggregated columns must appear in the GROUP BY clause (in standard SQL).
lessons.formula: SELECT group_col, AGG_FUNC(col) FROM table GROUP BY group_col; one result row per group.
lessons.worked_example: SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id; returns the number of employees in each department.
mistakes: Selecting non-aggregated columns that are not in GROUP BY
Grouping by the wrong column for the intended summary
Confusing WHERE (filters rows before grouping) with HAVING (filters groups)

lessons.title: Filtering Groups with HAVING
lessons.concept: HAVING filters groups after aggregation, often using aggregate conditions (e.g., COUNT(*) > 5). WHERE cannot use aggregate functions on grouped results; HAVING is used for conditions on aggregates or grouped outcomes.
lessons.formula: SELECT group_col, COUNT(*) FROM table GROUP BY group_col HAVING COUNT(*) > n;
lessons.worked_example: SELECT dept_id, AVG(salary) FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id HAVING AVG(salary) > 50000; returns only departments whose average salary exceeds 50000.
mistakes: Using WHERE with aggregate conditions instead of HAVING
Placing HAVING before GROUP BY in syntax
Applying conditions that should filter individual rows in HAVING instead of WHERE

practice.question: Which aggregate function returns the number of rows in a result set, including rows with NULL values?
practice.explanation: COUNT(*) counts all rows in the result set. COUNT(column_name) counts only non-NULL values in that column.

practice.question: What does the AVG function return?
practice.explanation: AVG(column) computes the arithmetic mean of the non-NULL values in that column.

practice.question: Which clause is used to group rows that have the same values in specified columns?
practice.explanation: GROUP BY groups rows sharing the same values in the specified column(s), typically so aggregate functions can produce per-group results.
practice.provenance: Authored original practice item; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

practice.question: Which clause is used to filter groups based on aggregate conditions (e.g., COUNT(*) > 3)?
practice.explanation: HAVING filters groups after aggregation and can use aggregate functions in its condition. WHERE filters individual rows before grouping and cannot use aggregates on grouped results.
practice.provenance: Authored original practice item; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

practice.question: Given table Sales(region, amount) with rows (North, 100), (South, 200), (North, 150), what does 'SELECT region, SUM(amount) FROM Sales GROUP BY region' return for North?
practice.explanation: Rows for North have amounts 100 and 150. SUM(amount) for North = 100 + 150 = 250.

practice.question: Which clause filters groups after aggregation?
practice.explanation: HAVING applies conditions to grouped/aggregated results (e.g. HAVING COUNT(*) > 5). WHERE filters rows before grouping and cannot directly use aggregate results in the same way.

practice.question: What does SELECT department, COUNT(*) FROM employees GROUP BY department; do?

options.B: Returns one row per department with number of employees in that department

practice.explanation: GROUP BY department forms groups of rows per department, and COUNT(*) computes the number of rows in each group, producing one summary row per department.

questions.explanation: MAX(column) is the aggregate function that returns the maximum (largest) value from the specified column.

questions.question: In a query using GROUP BY, which statement is true?

options.A: Non-aggregated columns in SELECT should be in GROUP BY
options.B: GROUP BY must come after ORDER BY
options.C: HAVING cannot be used with GROUP BY
options.D: Aggregate functions cannot be used with GROUP BY

questions.explanation: In standard SQL, columns in the SELECT list that are not aggregated must appear in the GROUP BY clause so each result row represents a well-defined group.

questions.question: You want to show departments having more than 10 employees. Which query fragment is correct?
questions.explanation: Conditions on aggregate results (like COUNT(*) per group) must be specified in the HAVING clause after GROUP BY, not in WHERE.

questions.question: A column has values 5, NULL, 15. What is the result of SUM of that column (ignoring non-numeric issues)?
questions.explanation: Aggregate functions like SUM ignore NULL values. SUM of 5 and 15 is 20.

questions.question: Which is the correct logical order for these clauses in a SELECT query: WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING?
questions.explanation: Rows are filtered by WHERE, then grouped by GROUP BY, then groups are filtered by HAVING. So the order is WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING.

questions.question: Which aggregate function returns the total of a numeric column?
questions.explanation: SUM adds numeric values in a column/group. COUNT returns number of rows/values, AVG returns mean, and MAX returns highest value.

questions.question: When using GROUP BY, non-aggregated columns in SELECT should generally be:

options.A: Arbitrary columns not in GROUP BY
options.B: Columns included in the GROUP BY clause (or functionally dependent, per SQL rules)

questions.explanation: Standard SQL requires selected non-aggregated expressions to be in GROUP BY so each group produces a single value for them; otherwise results are undefined/invalid in strict modes.
questions.provenance: Authored for BountyCode as original practice/question item; not scraped from third-party sources. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

questions.question: Which query finds departments having more than 10 employees?

options.A: SELECT department FROM employees WHERE COUNT(*) > 10 GROUP BY department;
options.B: SELECT department FROM employees GROUP BY department HAVING COUNT(*) > 10;
options.D: SELECT department FROM employees ORDER BY COUNT(*) > 10;

questions.explanation: The condition is on an aggregate (COUNT(*) per group), so it must be placed in HAVING after GROUP BY. WHERE cannot filter on aggregate results of the grouped set.
